name: spatial-partition
intent: Store every object in a structure indexed by its position so that neighbourhood queries visit only the objects near a point or region instead of scanning the whole population.
problem: Queries that ask 'what is near this position?' - collision checks, proximity and aggro radii, culling, spatial analytics - repeatedly scan every object: each query is linear in the population and a whole simulation step becomes quadratic, even though every object interacts only with the few objects next to it.
context: Per-object runtime systems and simulations - game worlds, crowd and particle solvers, location services, robotics - where objects are mobile, spread over space, and the queries are local (radius, region, k-nearest). The pattern applies once the population is large enough that a full scan dominates the frame or the request budget, and it requires a position-to-cell mapping and an update discipline that match how the objects move.
benefits: Query cost is proportional to the objects actually near the query region instead of to the total population, so neighbour checks stop being quadratic over a simulation step.
One index serves every spatial query - collision candidates, proximity, aggro, culling, pathfinding neighbourhoods - so query types and the partition structure evolve independently.
Coarse spatial pruning happens inside the structure: exact geometry tests run only on the candidates the cells produced.
Membership bookkeeping is centralised in insert/remove/update hooks, keeping movement policy separate from query policy.
Scales with object density rather than object count, and supports cheap negative answers (nothing in these cells means nothing nearby).
tradeoffs: Every move or teleport must update membership (remove plus reinsert, or a rebuild step); a missed update leaves stale entries that silently return wrong neighbours.
Degenerate distributions - most objects bunched into one cell - degrade toward the flat scan the pattern was meant to replace, so cell size and structure must match the world.
Extra memory and indirection: a container per occupied cell plus per-member references, with more allocation churn than a flat array of transforms.
Phase coupling: index updates must run in the same frame phase as movement (or be dirty-flagged and batched), adding ordering constraints to the update loop.
Debugging is less transparent: a wrong result may come from the distance predicate, the position-to-cell mapping or stale membership, and the candidate set is invisible at the call site.
Swapping the structure later (grid to quadtree or R-tree) touches every insert/remove/query caller unless the partition stays behind one interface.

participants.responsibility: Owns the cells and the position-to-cell mapping; exposes insert, remove and neighbour/region queries and hides which structure (grid, quadtree, R-tree) realizes them.
The partition unit that holds the members whose position or bounds fall into it; the unit of coarse pruning during a query.
The indexed object; it exposes a position (or bounds) and must have its membership updated whenever that position changes or it is destroyed.
Maps a world position or region to the cell coordinates that contain it; its granularity determines query cost, cell occupancy and worst-case behaviour.
Given a point, radius or region, visits only the cells that overlap it, then applies the exact predicate to the members found.
Whoever changes a position (movement system, physics step, teleport) keeps the partition in sync - remove and reinsert, or mark dirty and rebuild once per tick.

use_cases: Game worlds: collision, proximity and aggro checks between many moving entities each tick (bullets versus enemies, pickups, area effects).
Physics broadphase: pruning candidate pairs before narrow-phase tests where colliders move constantly.
Map and GIS services: 'all points within radius' and viewport queries over millions of features.
Crowd, flocking and particle simulations: neighbours within a radius for boids or social forces instead of all-pairs tests.
Spatial analytics and robotics: k-nearest or region queries over vehicles, sensors and delivery points, and occupancy grids for pathfinding.

Physics engines: Box2D's broadphase is a dynamic AABB tree (b2DynamicTree) whose fattened leaf boxes absorb small moves before reinsertion, and whose region queries and ray casts prune candidates before narrow-phase tests.

Location services: Redis geospatial indexes store members as 52-bit geohash scores in a sorted set (GEOADD) so GEOSEARCH answers circle and bounding-box proximity queries server-side instead of scanning members.

GIS and analytics databases: PostGIS prunes radius queries through a GiST spatial index (the index-aware ST_DWithin predicate checks bounding boxes before computing exact distances), and scikit-learn backs radius and k-nearest neighbour queries with KDTree and BallTree instead of all-pairs distances.
avoid_when: The population is small (a few dozen objects) or queried rarely: a linear scan is simpler and often faster than maintaining an index.
Queries are global rather than local ('process every entity'): partitioning only adds bookkeeping without pruning anything.
The runtime already maintains a broadphase for the same objects (physics engine, engine scene graph): query that index instead of building a second, divergent one.
The data is static and queried once per load: a sort or a database index answers the query without a live structure to keep in sync.
Positions are unbounded or streaming so no meaningful cell size exists: choose another spatial structure (hash grid, tree) or reconsider the query itself.
anti_patterns: Indexing objects but letting some movement paths bypass the index: ghost entries in old cells, queries that miss or double-report members.
One global cell size borrowed from a tutorial instead of measured against the world: worst-case cells degenerate to a full scan while most cells stay empty.
Rebuilding the whole partition every frame while an incremental remove-plus-reinsert (or dirty-flag) update would do.
Treating cell membership as the collision test: the partition yields candidates, the exact geometry predicate still has to run.
Growing one index for everything, including objects that never move (terrain, decorations) and are better served by a static structure.
design_principles: Separate the spatial index from the objects it indexes: the partition answers 'what is nearby?', the objects own their state.
Keep one insert/remove path per member so the position-to-cell mapping cannot drift from the authoritative positions.
Prune early: push coarse spatial predicates into the structure so exact geometry tests run on candidates only.
Match the data structure to the workload (uniform grid for evenly distributed movers, tree or hash for skewed or unbounded spaces) behind a stable query interface.
best_practices: Choose the cell size from the typical query radius (roughly one to two times it) and measure occupancy across the real distribution before shipping.
Update membership in the movement or teleport path - remove from the old cell and insert into the new one - or mark dirty and rebuild once per tick; never both silently.
Store ids or lightweight references in cells, not copies of entity state, and keep the partition replaceable behind the same query interface.
Bound the worst case: detect or cap overdense cells and degrade (smaller cells, hierarchical structure) instead of accepting a hidden full scan.
Query every cell overlapped by the region, deduplicate members that span several cells, then apply the exact predicate.
Use the same partition for spatial queries and spatial events (area triggers, collision candidates) so a second inconsistent index never appears.
sources: Nystrom, Game Programming Patterns (2014) - Spatial Partition, Optimization Patterns (the pattern's originating catalog).
